etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English startlen, stertlen, stertyllen (“to rush, stumble along”), from Old English steartlian (“to kick with the foot, struggle, stumble”), equivalent to start +‎ -le. Cognate with Old Norse stirtla (“to hobble, stagger”), Icelandic stirtla (“to straighten up, erect”). Compare also Middle English stertil (“hasty”). More at start.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move suddenly, or be excited, on feeling alarm; to start.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene v, page 1:
quote.text: Why shrinks the soul / Back on herself, and startles at destruction?

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], “A Proposal of Marriage”, in Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, page 127:
quote.text: He felt, too, that he was acting unjustly by Ethel: he had allowed a fortnight to elapse—he startled when he numbered up the days; it is strange how we allow them to glide imperceptibly away.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To excite by sudden alarm, surprise, or apprehension; to frighten suddenly and not seriously; to alarm; to surprise.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The supposition, at least, that angels do sometimes assume bodies need not startle us.

quote.citation: 1896, Joseph Conrad, chapter I, in An Outcast of the Islands, London: T. Fisher Unwin […], →OCLC, part I, page 10:
quote.text: Nothing could startle her, make her scold or make her cry. She did not complain, she did not rebel.

quote.citation: 1997, R. L. Stine, Say Cheese and Die, Again!:
quote.text: The high voice in the night air startled me. Without thinking, I started to run. Then stopped. I spun around, my heart heaving against my chest. And saw a boy. About my age.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To deter; to cause to deviate.

quote.citation: 1660, Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, The Life of Edward Earl of Clarendon, Lord High Chancellor of England:
quote.text: it would blast all their hopes, and startle all other princes from joining

quote.citation: 1922, Michael Arlen, “Ep./4/2”, in “Piracy”: A Romantic Chronicle of These Days:
quote.text: As they turned into Hertford Street they startled a robin from the poet's head on a barren fountain, and he fled away with a cameo note.

definitions.definition: A sudden motion or shock caused by an unexpected alarm, surprise, or apprehension of danger.

quote.citation: 1845, George Hooker Colton, James Davenport Whelpley, chapter 1, in The American review:
quote.text: The figure of a man heaving in sight amidst these wide solitudes, always causes a startle and thrill of expectation and doubt, similar to the feeling produced by the announcement of " a strange sail ahead" on shipboard, during a long voyage.
